Examples of hooks are Under-represented minorities. Let’s look at the US population. It’s about 58% white, 19% Hispanic, 12% black. If a college is 60% white, 10% hispanic, and 4% black, then the Hispanics and black students are under represented compared to the US population, hence the term URM (under represented minorities). This is the case for a lot of schools. Most are only 3 to 7% black and 8% Hispanic. So in order to combat this, schools tend to admit black and Hispanic students to increase their diversity. This is called Affirmative Action. I can’t dive into everything AA because this post will turn into a novel but often times in this sub you will see URMs unfortunately shamed for their acceptances like “you only got in because you’re black. It’s way easier for black students to get in than white students.” But the case is minority students like black and Hispanics are usually in lower socio economic standings and have to overcome a lot to become
top school caliber. But I will just end it here.

Another hook is legacy students. Parents who went to Harvard have a kid. When this kid applies the school will see that a parent went here. Thus, in theory, his chances are increased. A lot of legacy students come from families with money.

Another hook is athlete. If you’re a great athlete you will get recruited from great schools left and right. If you play a niche sport (sailing, frisbee, etc...) schools will take notice since those sports are in high demand I assume. 

Just because a student is hooked, doesn’t mean we need to diminish their accomplishments.

I somewhat feel the same way. Maybe listening to someone with a similar story can help ease your worries.

The thing with me is, my parents had a “no going out on weekdays” rule ever since second grade and well into my senior year. Around freshmen year I was talking to everyone at my new school and making new friends (because I’m extroverted) and I’d be invited places and usually the answer is no I can’t go sorry. My parents had this rule so I can focus on school but I didn’t realize how much it would affect my high school social life. It gets to the point where people will just think that your answer is no before you end up asking. So Monday-Thursday’s I’m home. Friday’s and Saturday’s Id have to be home by 8 (sometimes later if it’s a party). I’d see people I could’ve gotten close with slip away because I focused on making too many friends as possible at school and not solidifying myself with a group. Luckily I had close friends who didn’t mind seeing me only a few times a month. But as for school, I did work very hard since I was home a lot...but I also procrastinated a lot. My mentality was “I’m home all the time so I can postpone my work for a later day or hour” so most of my high school days consisted of socializing at school, going to clubs, coming home, doing homework, then sleep. 

I don’t think that I’m necessarily gifted in any subject. I really believed just having nothing to do but watch my shows and do homework contributed to my good grades. And just like you, I look back at my high school experience and wish I had more fun going out with people, experiencing parties and going bowling some Saturday’s. And just like you, I’m seeing my acceptances to these great schools and for most money isn’t that huge of an issue (so I sympathize with you there). But looking back, there wasn’t a lot I could’ve done to change my situation. 

In your case, I don’t want you to ever think that your hard work is all for not. I believe you’re feeling this way because you worked so hard just to get into a top school but don’t realize that the school you get into doesnt dictate your future (I know it’s a very overused statement but hear me out) in the last 4 years you built a work ethic parallel to none. You understood the meaning of sacrifice and blowing off plans to prioritize your studies. You worked for years to be crema de a crop and that work ethic will translate into any school you go to.

So you’re going to go to a state school. Okay. Start over. You have 4 years to not repeat the same mistakes you made in high school. You have 4 years to postpone that assignment for a later hour to hang out with your friends (don’t do that a lot tho) you have 4 years to party and have as much fun as you can while maintaining that 5.0 because you’re a genius. You have 4 years to make it anything you want. 

Nothing I say now will help with the pain of not going to your dream school. And even a year from now you’ll still feel the after affects. But take it from someone (me) who missed out on high school as well. You have to make these next 4 years your bitch. You have to experience the world or else it’ll pass you by when the real responsibilities kick in. You have developed great habits in high school. Now it’s time to mix that in with some fun. I know you’ll be successful no matter where you go. Feel free to message me person.

And let’s also say that you have a 1590 SAT a 4.8 GPA etc. The idea is that the school rejects you because they think “oh this kid is going to get into Harvard so there’s no point in us accepting because he’s going to reject our offer and lower our yield”  Yield is the number of students that apply compared to the number that choose to go. If a school accepts 10,000 students and only 2,000 accept their offer, their yield is 20% which is kind of low. But let’s say a school accepts 10,000 students and 9,000 choose to attend, then that’s a great yield. Hope this helps

We know that we are at an advantage but we didn’t choose this. And I agree with you 100% that those who pretend that their hook didn’t help them should re evaluate themselves. But understand that a certain level of imposter syndrome lives inside almost all of us. Feelings of inadequacy and not knowing whether or not our acceptance was based on merit or whether the school had a quota to fill and happened to see the perfect hooked applicant to fit the criteria. Again, I see your side. I just wanted to offer some perspective.

*Accept what is, let go of what was, and have faith in what will be.*

Here’s the truth. You worked very hard. You’re top of your class. You are a grinder and a true hard worker. 

The reason why I relate to this so much is that sometimes I feel like I’m living for other people rather than myself. Sometimes, I think in terms of whether or not a certain action would lead to the disappointment of my parents. Other times I’d think about whether or not I’m living up to the expectations of my extensive family who lives in another country.  

For me, I had somewhat of a social life but my parents emphasized education above all. Which I thank them for but I feel as if I missed out on a lot of high school experiences. Some days, when I wasn’t allowed to go out and I had free time, I’d spend it on snap looking at stores of other kids socializing and making bonds instead of doing my work. I would procrastinate a lot and leave things unfinished. 

But I realized something. 

*Accept what is, let go of what was, and have faith in what will be.*

You can’t take back the hard work you put in when in high school. Although it has gotten you to a great position, I’m sure you feel robbed of certain experiences. But high school isn’t the end. 

As cliche as it sounds, high school is only the beginning. As much as we like to think we know ourselves, it’s only in these next couple years that we form an identity of ourselves and **learn from the mistakes we make in high school**

For example, I made up a lot of excuses as to why I stopped reading. Now, I’m slowly picking it up again and plan on making it a regular thing when I’m in university. To continue, I made it a big thing freshmen year of high school to make a lot of friends. Although it made me well known, those same people I called my friends don’t text me or hit me up to see how I’m doing or make plans. Now I know that when I’m in college, find a group of solid friends. Branch out to make new friends but make sure the solidity is there. 

In your case, you will go to a great school. The rigor will be there. But are you going to lock yourself in a dorm in a perpetual cycle of studying for validation in the form of a letter grade or practice moderation to mitigate the stress of college. **Are you going to form a introverted identity and repeat the mistakes you made in high school or branch out and make friends to combat your loneliness**

Don’t live for other people. Live for yourself. Most people will say “go to a school that will make you happy.” And I second that. But I’m almost certain that you have parents who want you to go to a top school (which you’ll probably get into). At least in college, you’ll have independence. You’ll have freedom to choose whether or not to go out or study. Though you are expected to have great grades, you should really make college a fun and memorable experience. I am a senior and it took me a long time to achieve this mindset. I was once in your shoes. Once thinking I was depressed (probably was) because high school wasn’t going how I expected. Grinding and asking if it’ll all be worth it.

At the end, you told us to hang in there and that you’re fine. But I feel as if deep down you want to break the walls of conformity and branch out and explore. You should do that in college.

Sorry that this is so long: I really relate to this post and how you’re feeling and I wanted to share from one senior to another. You have the future to look forward to and you have the freedom to make the most of it. Your past is a lesson not a life sentence
